title: Slip stitch — the mover and the joiner
subtitle: No height, no loops left on the hook — the most versatile stitch you barely count
excerpt: Slip stitch is the shortest stitch in crochet. One move, no extra loops, no added height. It joins rounds, travels across stitches, and decorates surfaces. Worth knowing well beyond the beginner introduction.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet chapter, Project Gutenberg #20776 — the slip stitch as a joining and travelling move. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Vol. 1 (1886) — use of the slip stitch to close rounds and create picot chains.

glossaryTerms.definition: The shortest crochet stitch. Insert hook, yarn over, pull through the stitch and the loop on the hook in one movement — no height added.
A slip stitch into the first stitch or chain of a round to close the circle before starting the next round.

content.text: Slip stitch adds no height. You insert the hook, yarn over, and pull through both the stitch and the loop on the hook in one movement. The result is a flat join, a travelling step, or a decorative line — depending on where you put it.
The foundations tutorial covers the basic move. This tutorial covers the three distinct jobs the
slip stitch
does in real-world crochet: joining rounds cleanly, travelling across stitches without adding height, and creating surface decoration on finished fabric.
Job 1 — closing a round
When you work in rounds — a granny square, a circle, a hat brim — you close each round with a slip stitch into the top of the first stitch. This is the
joining round
. Done well, it lies flat and disappears into the fabric. Done loosely, it leaves a visible puckered join.
Work the round to the last stitch as the pattern states.
Insert the hook into the top of the first stitch of the round — the same stitch you began with, not the turning chain.
Yarn over.
Pull through both the stitch and the loop on the hook in one movement. One loop remains on the hook.
The round is closed. Chain up for the next round as the pattern states.

attrs.title: The common joining mistake
attrs.body: Joining into the turning chain instead of the first stitch is the most common error. The turning chain is not a stitch in most crochet patterns — if you join into it, your round spirals one stitch out. Count back from the turning chain and confirm which stitch is first.

content.text: Job 2 — travelling without height

Some patterns tell you to work slip stitches across a number of stitches to reposition without cutting the yarn. A shoulder seam on a garment, a granny-square border that starts mid-edge, or a motif join that begins at a different corner — all use this method.
Insert hook into the next stitch as normal.
Yarn over and pull through both the stitch and the loop on the hook.
Repeat across as many stitches as the pattern specifies.
Keep tension firm but not tight — travel slip stitches that pull too hard will gather the edge of the work.
Job 3 — surface decoration

Surface slip stitches are worked on top of a finished piece without the hook going through to the back. They draw raised lines: outlines on amigurumi faces, stripe patterns on flat fabric, faux seam lines on bags. Use a contrasting colour for visual impact.
Hold the new colour yarn at the back of the finished fabric.
Insert hook from front to back between two stitches and draw a loop through to the front.
Move one stitch along. Insert hook again from front to back.
Yarn over the working yarn and pull through both the fabric and the loop on the hook.
Continue along the planned line. The raised strand sits on the surface of the fabric.
Fasten off and weave both tails through the wrong side.

items.symptom: The join pulls the round tight
items.cause: Pulling the slip stitch too hard when closing a round
items.fix: Work the joining slip stitch with a slightly looser tension than the main stitches. The join should lie flat, not gather.

items.symptom: Travel slip stitches are visible as a ridge
items.cause: Tight tension or going through both loops when the pattern means only one
items.fix: Check whether the pattern specifies back-loop-only travel. Keep a consistent light tension across all travel stitches.

items.symptom: Surface line loops up off the fabric
items.cause: Tension too loose on surface slip stitches
items.fix: Slightly firmer tension on surface work keeps the strand lying flat. The strand should just touch the fabric, not float above it.

content.text: What to try next

Once the three uses of the slip stitch are comfortable, the join-as-you-go method for granny squares is the natural next step — it uses a joining slip stitch at the last round of each motif to assemble without sewing. The picot is the simplest decorative edge you can add using chains and slip stitches combined.
